title: I made a cruise ship management game with Claude Code writing most of the code and ElevenLabs doing the sound. Here's how it went
author: njbmartin
selftext:
Project Overboard is a Prison Architect style management game about a cruise ship: you lay out every deck, a yard of contractors builds it, then you hire the crew and take paying guests to sea. It's in Unity 6 and coming to Steam Early Access. Here's how the AI side worked.

**Code: Claude Code.** It wrote most of the code; I designed the game, set the rules and reviewed everything. Three things made that workable:

* A long project file of rules it reads every session: the simulation never touches Unity, runs on a fixed tick and must be deterministic; every number lives in a data asset; one class per file. Every design ruling I make goes in there too, so it doesn't relitigate them.
* Tests as the check rather than my eyes. The simulation runs headless, so thousands of EditMode tests run without opening the editor, and PlayMode "showcase" tests stage a scene and photograph it, so I can review screenshots instead of playing every change.
* Always running it. It compiles and tests in batchmode on every step, and a change isn't done until the tests pass.

It also helped write the text: the guests' thoughts, the Cruise Director's lines and the interface, all written to a voice guide with examples.

**Art: code, not image generation.** All the pixel art (the guests, the furniture, the walls, the port towns) is painted by editor scripts from style assets that hold every colour and size, and the port scenes are painted at runtime from their layouts. Claude wrote the painters; I judged the results from screenshots, over and over. No image model is involved anywhere.

**Sound: ElevenLabs.** About 200 sound effects and ambiences, the guests' voices (oohs, laughs, grumbles, by man, woman and child), the music, and the Cruise Director's announcements: about 400 lines, one take each, played over the tannoy. An import script trims each take, makes it as loud as the sound it replaces, and builds the game's sound catalogue from it. The original synthesised sounds stay behind each one as a fallback.

**The trailer** is filmed inside the game: PlayMode tests stage the ship, drive the camera and record every frame at a fixed step, so the footage is the real simulation with nothing faked.

What didn't go well: the AI is quick to build something that passes its own checks while missing the point. My first trailer ship packed every deck with dozens of blueprint restaurants and 29 bowling alleys on one floor. It looked nothing like a real ship, and it took a proper brief (the real ship's deck plans, a few large rooms each) to fix. The other problem is that it's built at real scale, and a full ship of guests is slow to simulate; that's next on my list.

Nothing is generated while you play; all of it was made beforehand.

Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5290110/Project\_Overboard/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5290110/Project_Overboard/)

Happy to go into any of it.
